In France, the national health insurance fund (Caisse nationale de l'Assurance Maladie) also runs
the workers' compensation insurance for most private-sector employees. It publishes the number of
recognised work accidents, commuting accidents and occupational diseases by sector, with the number
of employees, deaths, days off work and permanent incapacities. This notebook uses national totals
from 2005 and sector detail from 2015 to 2024. Read the module [README](../README.md) and
[data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)

base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/main/modules/fr-ameli-occupational-risks/data"
read_module <- function(folder, name, ...) {
  local <- file.path("..", "data", folder, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(base, folder, name), show_col_types = FALSE,
           ...)
}

# Claims, employees, frequency index, deaths, days off work and permanent incapacities
claims <- read_module("tidy", "claims_by_sector.csv.gz")
# Sector codes (NAF sections and subclasses) with English names
sectors <- read_module("tidy", "sectors.csv")
accident_causes <- read_module("tidy", "accident_causes.csv.gz")
diseases <- read_module("tidy", "occupational_diseases.csv.gz")
psych <- read_module("tidy", "psychological_disorders.csv")
costs <- read_module("tidy", "costs.csv")

national <- claims |> filter(level == "All sectors")
by_section <- claims |>
  filter(level == "Section") |>
  left_join(sectors |> filter(level == "Section") |> select(naf1, section_name), by = "naf1")
```

A **claim** is an accident or disease recognised by the insurance. For accidents, only those with
at least one day off work are counted. The **frequency index** is the number of accidents per 1,000
employees.

# Part 1. Twenty years of claims

```{r trend}
national |>
  filter(risk != "All risks") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, claims, colour = risk)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Recognised claims, France (general scheme)", x = NULL, y = "Claims", colour = NULL)

national |>
  filter(risk == "Work accidents") |>
  select(year, claims, employees, frequency_index)
```

**Questions**

1. How did the number of work accidents and the frequency index change from 2005 to 2024? Did the
   number of employees change too?
2. What happened in 2020, and why is the frequency index missing that year?
3. Commuting accidents did not fall like work accidents. Suggest a reason.

**Your answer:**



# Part 2. Sectors

```{r sectors}
by_section |>
  filter(risk == "Work accidents", year == 2024, !naf1 %in% c("T", "x")) |>
  mutate(days_per_claim = round(days_off_work / claims)) |>
  select(section_name, employees, claims, frequency_index, deaths, days_per_claim) |>
  arrange(desc(frequency_index))

by_section |>
  filter(risk == "Work accidents", naf1 %in% c("F", "H", "Q", "C", "N"), !is.na(frequency_index)) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, frequency_index, colour = section_name)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Work accidents per 1,000 employees", x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Which three sectors have the highest frequency of work accidents in 2024? Which has the most
   accidents in total?
2. Health and social work now has a frequency index similar to construction. What kinds of work in
   this sector cause accidents?
3. Days off work per accident differ between sectors. What does a high number of days per accident
   tell you that the frequency index does not?

**Your answer:**



# Part 3. Detailed sectors

The NAF classification has about 730 subclasses (the French version of the European NACE). The
data give accidents and employees for each.

```{r subclasses}
claims |>
  filter(level == "Subclass", risk == "Work accidents", year == 2024, employees >= 20000) |>
  left_join(sectors |> select(naf5, name_en), by = "naf5") |>
  select(naf5, name_en, employees, claims, frequency_index) |>
  arrange(desc(frequency_index)) |>
  head(15)
```

**Questions**

1. Which detailed activities have the highest frequency of work accidents among those with at least
   20,000 employees? What do the top ones have in common?
2. Why does this code only show subclasses with at least 20,000 employees? What happens to rates
   for very small subclasses?
3. Choose one activity in the top 15 and name its two most likely causes of accidents (Part 4 may
   help).

**Your answer:**



# Part 4. Causes

```{r causes}
accident_causes |>
  filter(level == "All sectors", risk == "Work accidents", year == 2024, cause != "All causes") |>
  arrange(desc(share_pct)) |>
  select(cause, share_pct)

accident_causes |>
  filter(level == "All sectors", risk == "Commuting accidents",
         cause == "Loss of control of a vehicle", vehicle != "All vehicles") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, share_pct, colour = vehicle)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Commuting accidents from losing control of a vehicle (% of all)", x = NULL,
       y = "%", colour = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. What share of work accidents are caused by manual handling? Propose prevention measures at two
   levels of the hierarchy of controls.
2. Which kind of vehicle has become a more common cause of commuting accidents since 2015? Suggest
   reasons.
3. The causes are shares (percentages), not counts. How would you calculate the number of accidents
   from manual handling in construction in 2024?

# Part 5. Occupational diseases

```{r diseases}
diseases |>
  filter(level == "All sectors", is.na(icd10_chapter)) |>
  select(year, disease_group, cases) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = cases)

psych |>
  filter(level == "All sectors") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, cases)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Recognised psychological disorders (occupational disease)", x = NULL,
       y = "Cases")
```

**Questions**

1. What share of recognised occupational diseases are musculoskeletal disorders? Why are they so
   common in compensation statistics?
2. Asbestos-related diseases are falling, but still about 2,000 a year, although asbestos was
   banned in France in 1997. Explain.
3. Psychological disorders (such as depression and burnout) are not on France's lists ("tableaux")
   of occupational diseases, so each case must be recognised individually. Their number grew more
   than fivefold from 2015 to 2024. Suggest reasons.

**Your answer:**



# Part 6. Deaths (ENVH 460/560)

```{r deaths}
national |>
  filter(risk %in% c("Work accidents", "Commuting accidents"), year >= 2015) |>
  select(year, risk, deaths) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = risk, values_from = deaths)

by_section |>
  filter(risk == "Work accidents", year >= 2022) |>
  group_by(section_name) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(deaths, na.rm = TRUE), employees = mean(employees, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(deaths_per_100000_per_year = round(1e5 * deaths / 3 / employees, 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(deaths)) |>
  head(8)
```

**Questions**

1. Deaths from work accidents jumped from about 550 in 2018 to over 700 in 2019. Is it likely that
   work became much more dangerous in one year? What else could explain a jump like this? (Look for
   Assurance Maladie's explanation of how deaths are counted.)
2. Which sectors have the most deaths, and which the highest death rate per 100,000 employees?
3. Many deaths at work in France are "malaises" (sudden deaths, often cardiovascular, at the
   workplace), which are presumed to be work accidents. How does this rule affect comparisons with
   countries that count only deaths caused by an injury?

**Your answer:**



# Part 7. Costs (ENVH 460/560)

```{r costs}
costs |>
  filter(risk != "All risks", cost_item != "All costs") |>
  group_by(year, risk) |>
  summarise(billion_eur = sum(amount_eur) / 1e9, .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, billion_eur, fill = risk)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Benefits paid, billion euros", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL)

costs |>
  filter(year == 2024, risk != "All risks") |>
  select(risk, cost_item, amount_eur) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = cost_item, values_from = amount_eur)
```

**Questions**

1. How much did the insurance pay in 2024, and what share went to occupational diseases? Why is the
   cost per case of an occupational disease much higher than of an accident?
2. In France, each employer's premium depends partly on the claims of its own sector or company.
   How can this encourage prevention, and how might it encourage under-reporting?
